# R328 — CPU pool host role and affinity after the fixed-worker matrix

Date: 2026-10-13 (JST). Read-only source and closed-record review of W at `e3c904e2e2247826f758ef0e682e2e7051152b86`, plus primary-source scheduling documentation. No build, test, model/GPU run, profiler, process inspection, Git operation, cleanup, or source edit. This report uses only the three explicitly authorized closed records under `main-long-decode128-root-v5/sample-{1,2,3}-workers-*-gu-unchanged/xe-timed1-on/record.json`; no other private record namespace was opened.

## Finding

The pool's thread layout is caller-led and intentionally pinned around one reserved physical core. On a six-core Ryzen 5600X with all 12 logical CPUs allowed, the host/caller is pinned to the first discovered physical core; pool worker (i) is pinned to physical core index (i), with the default first worker starting at index 1. The supplied closed ready-thread-affinity evidence reports the expected host on CPU 0, workers on CPUs 1..N, and 19 threads allowed the full 12-CPU mask. That shows the service's affinity inheritance and the pool's intended placement; it does not prove that CPU 0 is exclusively available to this process or identify its cycle share.

With `host_works=true`, the caller joins the same dynamic row-task drain as workers, all contending on one atomic claim head. In the tested setting, five workers plus caller means six participants and 18 tasks per eligible phase. The caller does useful CPU expert rows while the five workers do theirs, then participates in the completion/park boundaries. With `host_works=false`, the caller does no pool row work and spins for worker completion; it still performs coordination. `--no-host-worker` is therefore a useful distinct placement/participation arm, but it changes effective participants (and automatic tasks) together. It is not a pure affinity-only toggle.

The current closed samples are a screening result, not a worker-count conclusion: worker 5, 3, and 4 each had one exact 32K-input / 128-token run with the same 18 tasks and otherwise fixed setup. Supplied engine prefill/decode values were respectively 391.515 / 3.9993, 388.948 / 7.7539, and 375.444 / 8.4747 (decode tok/s). Each was Main-verified PASS, normal QUIT, no ownership error, and fault-free; reported 128-token output/LP5 equality is bounded to that reported output. These one-off samples do not justify selecting a worker count. In particular, per-request output-history differences can alter decode work, and exact generated output is not a universal quality gate.

## Source-grounded thread/critical-path mechanics

- `physical_cores()` enumerates the caller's allowed affinity mask, keeps the first allowed logical CPU for each sysfs package/core pair, and falls back to all allowed logical CPUs if topology files are unavailable. `physical_cores(true)` drops the first discovered core. Workers are created at pool construction and each lambda applies its requested singleton affinity before entering `worker()`. Requests above the discovered remaining-core count produce `core=-1` and run unpinned; pin failures are not surfaced by `pin_this_thread`.
- `SessionLoopScratch::init` pins its calling thread to `physical_cores(false)[0]` and restores the saved mask in `free()`. In the serving path this is the session-loop caller. So the nominal reservation only applies when this scratch lifecycle encloses the pool work on that same thread. The explicitly supplied affinity report supports that inheritance for this service invocation.
- In `run_phase`, all workers first park, the host publishes one epoch, then the host drains if enabled, and all participants share the same atomic job head. The host waits until jobs are done and workers have parked again. `wait_parked` and `wait_done` are tight `_mm_pause()` loops with a 1024-spin cadence for time checks; workers spin while waiting for an epoch and can enter condition-variable sleep after `STRATA_POOL_SPIN_US`. Current reports say this setting was unchanged. The work loop itself is not a GPU poll loop.
- For native batched MoE, each phase divides all rows across the batch into equal contiguous tasks; workers (and optionally host) dynamically claim them. The default task count is three per participating thread, capped by rows. Fixed `--pool-tasks 18` keeps the count stable across the 3/4/5 worker matrix, so the participant-count contrast also changes how many threads contend for the same 18 tasks. Fewer workers can mean fewer claimers but longer per-thread work; more workers can lower service time or add scheduling/cache contention. Source alone does not resolve which effect dominates.
- The serving/session caller has sequential responsibilities around the pool callback: waiting on GPU boundary/doorbell state, arranging/handing off expert work, then the pool callback and subsequent copy/flag/next-segment steps as applicable. With atomic-coherent polling disabled, do not assume CPU and GPU are concurrently polling the same atomics or claim that an affinity change improves that overlap. The pool timings combine useful worker compute with claims and coordination; they do not report per-thread busy time or isolate cache/memory contention.

Thus, host work can help fill the otherwise reserved core during CPU expert rows, but the caller cannot simultaneously advance its outer session-loop duties while synchronously draining those rows. Worker pinning constrains where its own thread executes; it does not reserve those CPUs from unrelated service/runtime threads, nor set GPU-side placement. The 19-thread allowed-mask observation is not a count of active Strata workers.

## Existing knob sequence and safe inference

R270 already recommended comparing fixed worker counts before task grain and cautioned against interpreting cumulative pool timings as request-local CPU work. R328 adds one useful distinction: compare host participation only after the worker matrix identifies a stable candidate, because host participation changes both work distribution and host-side coordination/availability. Keep the agreed no-concurrent-polling configuration, >=32,768 actual input positions, identical context/cache/profile/route settings, 18 tasks, 128-token continuation, and request/output policy fixed. Use multiple paired fresh-process samples and compare distributions, failures, exact generated outputs, and decode timing; a single best sample is not evidence.

After the worker matrix, a meaningful existing one-axis question is caller participation: at a candidate worker count, compare default host work against `--no-host-worker`, keeping explicit `--pool-tasks 18` so automatic task-count coupling is removed. This still tests the combined effect of caller CPU contribution and its completion-wait role, not a pure host-affinity change. Only if that contrast is consistent should task count be tested as a separate axis (auto vs nearby explicit values), and only if timing instrumentation distinguishes CPU row service from wait/dispatch should further source work be proposed. A new affinity knob or CPU reservation policy is not supported by current evidence.

No unsupported causal claim follows from the current three samples. Their variance and output-history scopes leave open task history, worker scheduling, row/cache locality, and host dispatch contributions. The current data do not show a GPU hang or establish a new coordination problem.

## Primary-source context

Intel VTune's threading guidance separates active spin, synchronization wait, scheduler overhead, and oversubscription, and recommends inspecting those categories before tuning. It supports measuring worker and coordination behavior independently; its general advice is not a Strata-specific performance result ([Intel VTune Threading Efficiency View](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/vtune-profiler/user-guide/2025-4/threading-efficiency-view.html)).

Official llama.cpp/ggml provides a comparable CPU pool with a shared atomic chunk counter, barrier counters, affinity/NUMA handling and an explicit polling parameter. It is a useful design comparator for the kinds of controls and costs to measure, but different kernels and scheduling do not imply a transferable setting or speedup ([ggml CPU threadpool source](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c), [llama.cpp CPU scheduling options](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/common/common.cpp)).

Official CUDA and HIP guides explain that asynchronous device work may proceed while host code performs other work, and host/device synchronization should be scoped to the needed stream/event. These establish the general host-work opportunity and synchronization requirement, not that this Strata path gets concurrency under its current atomic/polling caps ([CUDA asynchronous execution](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/02-basics/asynchronous-execution.html), [HIP asynchronous concurrent execution](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/HIP/en/docs-10.1.0/how-to/hip_runtime_api/asynchronous.html)). oneTBB's arena API is a contrast where caller participation and concurrency limits can be explicitly reserved; adopting that runtime is outside this research and offers no evidence of benefit here ([oneTBB task_arena](https://uxlfoundation.github.io/oneTBB/main/specification/source/task_scheduler/task_arena/task_arena_cls.html)).
